Borer Beetles

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A tiny alien beetle is threatening to change our urban landscapes forever....

Unique Selling Point:
The Polyphagous Shothole Borer (PSHB), is a sesame seed-sized beetle that infests more than 200 tree species from 58 families. The beetle bores into the tree and lays its eggs. But it is not this damage that kills the tree. The beetle travels with a range of symbiotic fungi and it is one strain of the fungus, which the larvae feeds on once they hatch that causes harm to the tree. A dedicated team of scientists - under the leadership of Prof Wilhelm de Beer from FABI is working to find a way to evict the PSHB from Urban forests, our fruit trees and natural forests.

Summary:
OPENING LINK - trees - Thhis is the most beautiful time of the year in Johannesburg, but imagine this view without the trees.
A tiny alien is infecting our trees, a potential catastrophy for urban and natural forests.

Seq - Tree pests are nothing new - the price we pay for globalisation…

Dedicated team at Pretoria University - FABI
Some of FABI Successes…. but now they have a new enemy...
Trudy Paap discovered the beetle. Wilhelm de Beer and his team are tracking the process. - we look at the beetle, how to identify, how it reproduces, the symbiotic fungus and damage caused. We also look at the people and the work they put in - the hours of dedication it takes to fight such a tiny enemy - they will also show us a process of innoculating trees which they are currently testing. They will show the beetle under the microscope, DNA sequencing, symbiotic fungus.

Spread of the beetle - KNP, Northern Cape, KZN, Western Cape, Limpopo… How it spreads

Food security? We chat to FABI about the possible infestation of fruit tree crops. (maize and wheat are fine, but many fruit trees are suseptable)

Joburg, threat to the Urban forest - speak to City Parks — what people must do if they have infested trees. How to minimise the threat. WHAT NOT TO DO. Introduction of dedicated sites where people can take felled trees.

Hylton Fryar - App developed for reporting possible infestation - more than 300 users of the app - key to identifying the spread of the beetle.

Neil Hill - Joburg Urban Forest Alliance - shows infected trees. Felling

Back to FABI, what they do when people report the infestation. The future - how the beetle can be stopped - possible biocontrol — Biologists think that minute parasitic wasps, which are known to attack ambrosia beetles in their native range, could be introduced to South Africa, but these first need to be thoroughly studied to make sure they won’t also attack indigenous South African beetles. Threat to indigenous forests.




Further information:
Protecting Trees

The price we pay for globalisation is that pests and diseases have access to new habitats and can quickly colonise a new area. Tree pests are nothing new to South Africa, we have been fighting bugs like the Ecalyptus snout beetle and the Sirex woodwasp for many decades. In fact, since 1997 we've had a dedicated team of superheroes that look after the health of our trees – commercial tree crops, ornamental trees for gardening and urban greening as well as our indigenous forests.

FABI is the Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute at the University of Pretoria. The entire team is made up of more than 200 people and include professors, research post graduates and supporting staff. Their main goal is to ensure the health of all our trees.

FABI obviously does a lot of work for commercial plantations and various insect pests have been identified and treated over the years. It's a lengthy process which starts with samples taken in the field. The pests need to be identified 100% with DNA analysis, sometimes there is a symbiont fungus that accompanies the insect, this too needs to be identified. At FABI they have test sites to purposefully infect trees to see the effects and test possible counter-pests. There is a DNA sequencing facility and various labs where nematodes and possible pathogens are bred and tested.

Finding a biocontrol agent that is target specific is a lengthy process. Some of the ongoing projects include the Cossid moth which infects the Eucalyptus nitens trees used in commercial plantations. The moth bores tunnels in the trunk of the tree to lay its eggs. In order to control the spread of the Cossid moth, FABI engineered an artificial pheromone used to lure and trap the moths during their flight season. The sirex Woodwasp is another headache for the commercial forestry sector. This wasp attacks certain Pine species and FABI helped develop a biological control agent – a parasitic nematode that only feeds on the specific fungus that the woodwasp injects into the tree. This nematode is mass produced at FABI and then used to inoculate trees with. The Blue Gum Gall Wasp female lays her eggs in young Eucalyptus trees which stunts growth of the tree. So far 4 wasp parasitoids have been identified but they are still in the testing phase before these can be used in the field.

But the FABI team are faced with a new challenge. Unlike many other pests who hone in on a specific plant species or family, the Polyphagous Shothole Borer (PSHB), is a sesame seed-sized beetle that infests more than 200 tree species from 58 families. The beetle bores into the tree and lays its eggs. But it is not this damage that kills the tree. The beetle travels with a range of symbiotic fungi and it is one strain of the fungus, which the larvae feeds on once they hatch that causes harm to the tree.

The PSHB/fungus combination poses a threat to a range of tree crops, like avocado, macadamia, pecan, peach, orange and certain vines. It has also been found on indigenous species like cabbage tree, Outeniqua yellowwood, kruidjie-roer-my-nie, coral trees, monkey plum, some species of acacia, keurboom and paper bark. The biggest concern thus far is the threat to Johannesburg's urban forest. Many ornamental trees have been infected in the Sandton Parkhurst area, as well as in Soweto where 300,000 trees were planted in 2010 as part of the Greening Soweto project.

The pregnant female beetle can fly up to 1km which facilitates the spread. Infestations have been found in Bloemfontein, George & Knysna.

The PSHB was first discovered in South Africa in 2007 by Dr Trudy Paap at the KZN Botanical Gardens in Pietermaritzburg and she is still involved in the research.

Meet the superheroes at FABI that are fighting this new threat:

At the helm of fighting this PSHB are Professors Brett Hurley, Wilhelm de Beer and Noelani van den Berg . They also form part of the Ambrosia Beetle Working Group that has recently been established to bring various stakeholders together (Including DAFF, Joburg City Parks and the Plant Healthy Early Warnings System).

Prof Wilhelm de Beer is a mycologist/fungal biologist that focusses on the fungal symbiont that comes with the borer beetle. This fungus is what actually ends up killing trees. De Beer oversees the DNA sequencing of the fungus to establish if different specimens found in different locations across SA (and the world) are indeed the same strain. Once the fungus is 100% identified they can work on finding a natural enemy.

Prof Brett Hurley is a researcher focussing on insect pests in Forest Trees. He focusses on finding a biocontrol agent for the PSHB, by looking at factors such as host resistance (i.e. which trees the bugs DO NOT eat) and insect-microbe interactions.

Prof Van Den Berg runs the Fruit Tree Biotechnology Programme at FABI. At the moment there are no infestations of fruit trees by PSHB in South Africa, and she and her team are working on keeping our trees safe – i.e. preventative measures. Together they continually monitor the spread of the beetle across the country, and assess the risks to crop trees, commercial forests and indigenous forests.

Dr Paap is also based at FABI and is part of the International Plant Sentinel Network, which serves as an early warning system to notify scientists of new pests and pathogens to a specific country. The IPSN is an international network, linking botanical gardens and arboreta and plant health scientists. Dr Paap's work is all about detecting threats early so plans can be put in place to mitigate the threats.

Scientists don't have all the answers yet, but the race is on to find out how exactly the symbiotic process between the PSHB and the associated fungus works and what makes some trees resistant and others not.

Additional Info:

Contrary to the Daily Maverick article, Joburg City Parks is quite involved behind the scenes. Adelaide Chokoe is the organisation's arboriculturist and is also part of the Ambrosia Beetle Working Group. The Joburg Tree Society is also actively involved, identifying affected trees, and feeding the information to FABI. At the moment the focus of the media is on Johannesburg City's trees. There are many worried gardeners and the idea is not to create a panic. Insecticides and fungicides DO NOT WORK, even though there are those on Facebook that claims it does. Affected trees need to be cut down, chipped or burnt to limit the spread of the PSHB.

The greater concern is of course our tree crops and natural forests. In the USA and Israel they have experienced large die-offs of trees like Avocado as a result of infestation.

There are some concerns about the widespread castor bean in the KZN region. It is an important reproductive host and could potentially act as a corridor for invasion across urban and agricultural habitats.

Press Release:


Evicting Alien Borer Beetles
For South Africa, globalisation has come at a price – pests like the tiny polyphagous shot hole borer beetle are invading fruit trees, natural forests around the country, and one of the world’s largest urban forests – Johannesburg. Now the Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute in Pretoria is working against the clock to develop a strategy against the infestation. Carte Blanche asks whether the solution will come in time to save our landscape and tree crops form the out of control beetle.
Producer: Stenette Grosskopf
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


BORER BEETLE

MAC LINK
This time of the year Joburg is postcard perfect – Jacarandas are in full bloom and our urban forest is lush. Now imagine what life in the city would be if all of these trees would disappear.
V/O
The increase in tree pests and diseases from foreign parts of the world is one of the prices we pay for globalisation. It's getting easier and easier for bugs, bacteria and fungi to get here and find a suitable host to thrive on.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
Many more ships now visit our harbours. They bring in wood, they export wood, but just on the pallets and pieces of wood that come in, lots of these forest insects can actually enter the country.
V/O
The Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute, or FABI, based at the University of Pretoria is a leading research institution, that has been working on tree pests and diseases for more than 20 years. Prof Wilhelm de Beer specialises in pest insects and has helped to identify a number of natural enemies for some of the bigger tree threats.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
We especially have a very strong biological control programme on one pine pest in SA, but similarly we have 3 biocontrol agents that we developed, and that we produce now for the industry, on eucalyptus pests.
V/O
One of our more recent unwanted immigrants from South East Asia is the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle that has established itself in pockets around the country. Prof de Beer and his team have been studying the beetle and regularly analyse infected tree samples.

So we've got a whole bunch that we've collected inside this little tube.

MAC: Is this how small they are?

Ja.That's how small they are.

MAC: These are the actual beetles that can bring down an entire tree?

Ja. There is thousands upon thousands of them – in a branch like this you can get probably a couple of hundred.
V/O
Unlike other borer beetles that attack dying or stressed trees, the Shot Hole Borer infests living trees. They burrow tiny holes through the bark, deep into the stem of the tree... and they invade a whole variety of tree species.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
That is the scary part about the shot hole borer, it goes for everything – big trees, small trees, thin trees, thick bark, branches, stems... In California they reported it on more than 200 host tree species. In South Africa already we have found it on 80 different tree species.
V/O
Amazingly they are able to bore their way through a variety of obstacles...
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
This little bugger is really ferocious. In terms of what it can do... I didn't realise it until I had a sample in a little ziplock bag in my desk. The beetle actually ate through the plastic into a varnished, laminated wood bookshelf. I really got scared.
V/O
The Shot Hole Borer travels with a fungus, which grows in the tunnels.
Shamus
They deposit them in the tree and then it grows and this is their primary food source...
V/O
Under the microscope one can clearly see the white spores growing in the tunnels... The tree's vascular system, a series of tiny tubes that allows moisture and nutrients to flow through it, then becomes blocked by the fungus and in many cases the tree eventually dies.
LINK
The Shot Hole Borer Beetle was “officially” discovered last year at the KZN Botanical Gardens in Pietermaritzburg, although experts believe that they may have been flying under the radar for a number of years.
V/O
In Johannesburg the Shot Hole Borer was first confirmed at the beginning of the year. Resident, Hilton Fryer started alerting City Parks and neighbours when several of his own trees started dying.
Hilton Fryer
I would try to raise awareness with people but they don't really kind of connect with the problem because they haven't really noticed their own trees dying yet.
V/O
Neil Hill is an arborist based in Joburg and easily identifies the infected trees.
Neil Hill
The most obvious signs are the tiny little holes that you'll see in the stem and the lower parts of the canopy.

MAC: So these ones over here?

Ja, these ones over here.
V/O
In some species like Oak, the thick bark masks the holes.
Neil Hill
The darker patches you see there are also a symptom. That's a reaction to a borer getting into the tree and the fungi growing around the entry wound.
V/O
To help track infected trees, Fryer developed the Tree Survey app - available for apple and android – which you can download to report an infected tree.
Hilton
The nice thing that we can actually do is, when they report it, they can not only give us their physical location within the app, they can submit photographs, give us descriptions and then they open a channel where we can do in-app communication....
V/O
Trees in city parks and on pavements are the responsibility of the local municipalities
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
Our local governments have never had to deal with anything like this, so this is something completely new and they're completely not prepared and equipped to deal with type of stuff.
Ben Masalesa
Everybody is looking for a remedy – that is internationally. They're looking for a remedy for that.
V/O
Senior Training Facilitator at Joburg City Parks, Ben Masalesa says the outbreaks in Joburg are contained and there is no reason to panic.
Ben Masalesa
Interestingly we don't have large scale dying of trees, we still have those London Plane trees, especially on Jan Smuts Ave, they're still standing. Some of them a showing a bit of resistance to the beetle because they are thriving.
V/O
But the beetles can fly up to a kilometer and in some Johannesburg suburbs you can see rows of dying trees. There are also reports of infestation in Pietermaritzburg and Durban, and all the way up the coast, almost to Richards Bay. Even more worrisome are the infected trees near our indigenous forests on the Garden Route
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
In Knysna they had to cut down Oak trees this size that was killed by the beetle. We have one report from Bloemfontein, and then in the Pecan nut orchards in the Northern Cape we have some reports...
V/O
In the USA and Israel, macadamia and avocado crops are under attack and understandably tree crop growers are nervous. Fabi is conducting tests on Pecan trees to see which variety is less affected by this specific fungus.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
So what we physically do is we take the fungus that comes from the beetles. And we make holes in the tree and infect the tree with the fungus.
V/O
And in about six weeks' time they'll be able to see the effects of the fungus and advise the pecan growers on which cultivar of tree to plant in the future.
V/O
There is currently no cure or treatment for infected trees and experts warn against the use of untested chemicals.
Neil Hill
Borer is typically a very difficult problem to solve and in particular in this case because this shot hole borer travels so deep into the stem of the tree it is even more difficult. So treatments are still experimental and are not guaranteed.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
My gut feeling is we should rather look at management strategies where governments – national level and also on a local level become involved in especially removing, in a responsible way the susceptible trees in which the beetle reproduce.
V/O
For now the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle is here to stay and many trees will die unless we can effectively manage the outbreak.
Prof Wilhelm de Beer
The beetle is not going to kill all the trees in the country. That's a fact. So we're not going to lose all our trees. But we're going to see impact in certain areas. Personally my biggest concern is really in terms of our native trees because there it is very unpredictable. We have found it on more than 30 native tree species in the country. And there the impact might not be as visible initially, but it might dramatically change ecosystems by taking out keystone tree species in particular ecosystems.




PROMO 10”
A tiny invasive borer beetle is attacking some of our urban, native and crop trees with potential devastating effects. Are the experts and authorities geared for this invasion?


PROMO 15”
UPSOUND: Wilhelm
Very seldom a serious pest will attack a lot of different host trees. And that is the scary part about the shot hole borer, it goes for everything...

More than 80 trees species in SA have been affected by the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle. What is being done to safeguard our trees?


PROMO 15”
It's not just Joburg's trees that are affected by the invasive Shot Hole Borer Beetle.

UPSOUND: Wilhelm
Down in George and Knysna area, the impact is immense, in Knysna they had to cut down Oak trees this size that was killed by the beetle.

How does one stop a tiny beetle with a ferocious appetite?



PROMO 30”
The invasive Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer beetle is in our cities and seems to be spreading.



UOSOUND: Wilhelm
In South Africa already we have found it on 80 different tree species.

Infected trees are identified by tiny little holes in the trunk and branches.

UPSOUND: Hilton
I would try to raise awareness with people but they don't really kind of connect with the problem because they haven't really noticed their own trees dying yet.

How will city and natural landscapes change as this beetle continues to spread it's wings?

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 08 November 2018 Press Release: Evicting Alien Borer Beetles For South Africa, globalisation has come at a price – pests like the tiny polyphagous shot hole borer beetle are invading fruit trees, natural forests around the country, and one of the world’s largest urban forests – Johannesburg. Now the Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute in Pretoria is working against the clock to develop a strategy against the infestation. Carte Blanche asks whether the solution will come in time to save our landscape and tree crops form the out of control beetle. Producer: Stenette Grosskopf Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Script: BORER BEETLE MAC LINK This time of the year Joburg is postcard perfect – Jacarandas are in full bloom and our urban forest is lush. Now imagine what life in the city would be if all of these trees would disappear. V/O The increase in tree pests and diseases from foreign parts of the world is one of the prices we pay for globalisation. It's getting easier and easier for bugs, bacteria and fungi to get here and find a suitable host to thrive on. Prof Wilhelm de Beer Many more ships now visit our harbours. They bring in wood, they export wood, but just on the pallets and pieces of wood that come in, lots of these forest insects can actually enter the country. V/O The Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute, or FABI, based at the University of Pretoria is a leading research institution, that has been working on tree pests and diseases for more than 20 years. Prof Wilhelm de Beer specialises in pest insects and has helped to identify a number of natural enemies for some of the bigger tree threats. Prof Wilhelm de Beer We especially have a very strong biological control programme on one pine pest in SA, but similarly we have 3 biocontrol agents that we developed, and that we produce now for the industry, on eucalyptus pests. V/O One of our more recent unwanted immigrants from South East Asia is the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle that has established itself in pockets around the country. Prof de Beer and his team have been studying the beetle and regularly analyse infected tree samples. So we've got a whole bunch that we've collected inside this little tube. MAC: Is this how small they are? Ja.That's how small they are. MAC: These are the actual beetles that can bring down an entire tree? Ja. There is thousands upon thousands of them – in a branch like this you can get probably a couple of hundred. V/O Unlike other borer beetles that attack dying or stressed trees, the Shot Hole Borer infests living trees. They burrow tiny holes through the bark, deep into the stem of the tree... and they invade a whole variety of tree species. Prof Wilhelm de Beer That is the scary part about the shot hole borer, it goes for everything – big trees, small trees, thin trees, thick bark, branches, stems... In California they reported it on more than 200 host tree species. In South Africa already we have found it on 80 different tree species. V/O Amazingly they are able to bore their way through a variety of obstacles... Prof Wilhelm de Beer This little bugger is really ferocious. In terms of what it can do... I didn't realise it until I had a sample in a little ziplock bag in my desk. The beetle actually ate through the plastic into a varnished, laminated wood bookshelf. I really got scared. V/O The Shot Hole Borer travels with a fungus, which grows in the tunnels. Shamus They deposit them in the tree and then it grows and this is their primary food source... V/O Under the microscope one can clearly see the white spores growing in the tunnels... The tree's vascular system, a series of tiny tubes that allows moisture and nutrients to flow through it, then becomes blocked by the fungus and in many cases the tree eventually dies. LINK The Shot Hole Borer Beetle was “officially” discovered last year at the KZN Botanical Gardens in Pietermaritzburg, although experts believe that they may have been flying under the radar for a number of years. V/O In Johannesburg the Shot Hole Borer was first confirmed at the beginning of the year. Resident, Hilton Fryer started alerting City Parks and neighbours when several of his own trees started dying. Hilton Fryer I would try to raise awareness with people but they don't really kind of connect with the problem because they haven't really noticed their own trees dying yet. V/O Neil Hill is an arborist based in Joburg and easily identifies the infected trees. Neil Hill The most obvious signs are the tiny little holes that you'll see in the stem and the lower parts of the canopy. MAC: So these ones over here? Ja, these ones over here. V/O In some species like Oak, the thick bark masks the holes. Neil Hill The darker patches you see there are also a symptom. That's a reaction to a borer getting into the tree and the fungi growing around the entry wound. V/O To help track infected trees, Fryer developed the Tree Survey app - available for apple and android – which you can download to report an infected tree. Hilton The nice thing that we can actually do is, when they report it, they can not only give us their physical location within the app, they can submit photographs, give us descriptions and then they open a channel where we can do in-app communication.... V/O Trees in city parks and on pavements are the responsibility of the local municipalities Prof Wilhelm de Beer Our local governments have never had to deal with anything like this, so this is something completely new and they're completely not prepared and equipped to deal with type of stuff. Ben Masalesa Everybody is looking for a remedy – that is internationally. They're looking for a remedy for that. V/O Senior Training Facilitator at Joburg City Parks, Ben Masalesa says the outbreaks in Joburg are contained and there is no reason to panic. Ben Masalesa Interestingly we don't have large scale dying of trees, we still have those London Plane trees, especially on Jan Smuts Ave, they're still standing. Some of them a showing a bit of resistance to the beetle because they are thriving. V/O But the beetles can fly up to a kilometer and in some Johannesburg suburbs you can see rows of dying trees. There are also reports of infestation in Pietermaritzburg and Durban, and all the way up the coast, almost to Richards Bay. Even more worrisome are the infected trees near our indigenous forests on the Garden Route Prof Wilhelm de Beer In Knysna they had to cut down Oak trees this size that was killed by the beetle. We have one report from Bloemfontein, and then in the Pecan nut orchards in the Northern Cape we have some reports... V/O In the USA and Israel, macadamia and avocado crops are under attack and understandably tree crop growers are nervous. Fabi is conducting tests on Pecan trees to see which variety is less affected by this specific fungus. Prof Wilhelm de Beer So what we physically do is we take the fungus that comes from the beetles. And we make holes in the tree and infect the tree with the fungus. V/O And in about six weeks' time they'll be able to see the effects of the fungus and advise the pecan growers on which cultivar of tree to plant in the future. V/O There is currently no cure or treatment for infected trees and experts warn against the use of untested chemicals. Neil Hill Borer is typically a very difficult problem to solve and in particular in this case because this shot hole borer travels so deep into the stem of the tree it is even more difficult. So treatments are still experimental and are not guaranteed. Prof Wilhelm de Beer My gut feeling is we should rather look at management strategies where governments – national level and also on a local level become involved in especially removing, in a responsible way the susceptible trees in which the beetle reproduce. V/O For now the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle is here to stay and many trees will die unless we can effectively manage the outbreak. Prof Wilhelm de Beer The beetle is not going to kill all the trees in the country. That's a fact. So we're not going to lose all our trees. But we're going to see impact in certain areas. Personally my biggest concern is really in terms of our native trees because there it is very unpredictable. We have found it on more than 30 native tree species in the country. And there the impact might not be as visible initially, but it might dramatically change ecosystems by taking out keystone tree species in particular ecosystems. PROMO 10” A tiny invasive borer beetle is attacking some of our urban, native and crop trees with potential devastating effects. Are the experts and authorities geared for this invasion? PROMO 15” UPSOUND: Wilhelm Very seldom a serious pest will attack a lot of different host trees. And that is the scary part about the shot hole borer, it goes for everything... More than 80 trees species in SA have been affected by the Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer Beetle. What is being done to safeguard our trees? PROMO 15” It's not just Joburg's trees that are affected by the invasive Shot Hole Borer Beetle. UPSOUND: Wilhelm Down in George and Knysna area, the impact is immense, in Knysna they had to cut down Oak trees this size that was killed by the beetle. How does one stop a tiny beetle with a ferocious appetite? PROMO 30” The invasive Polyphagous Shot Hole Borer beetle is in our cities and seems to be spreading. UOSOUND: Wilhelm In South Africa already we have found it on 80 different tree species. Infected trees are identified by tiny little holes in the trunk and branches. UPSOUND: Hilton I would try to raise awareness with people but they don't really kind of connect with the problem because they haven't really noticed their own trees dying yet. How will city and natural landscapes change as this beetle continues to spread it's wings?

metadata.Further information: Protecting Trees The price we pay for globalisation is that pests and diseases have access to new habitats and can quickly colonise a new area. Tree pests are nothing new to South Africa, we have been fighting bugs like the Ecalyptus snout beetle and the Sirex woodwasp for many decades. In fact, since 1997 we've had a dedicated team of superheroes that look after the health of our trees – commercial tree crops, ornamental trees for gardening and urban greening as well as our indigenous forests. FABI is the Forestry and Agricultural Biotechnology Institute at the University of Pretoria. The entire team is made up of more than 200 people and include professors, research post graduates and supporting staff. Their main goal is to ensure the health of all our trees. FABI obviously does a lot of work for commercial plantations and various insect pests have been identified and treated over the years. It's a lengthy process which starts with samples taken in the field. The pests need to be identified 100% with DNA analysis, sometimes there is a symbiont fungus that accompanies the insect, this too needs to be identified. At FABI they have test sites to purposefully infect trees to see the effects and test possible counter-pests. There is a DNA sequencing facility and various labs where nematodes and possible pathogens are bred and tested. Finding a biocontrol agent that is target specific is a lengthy process. Some of the ongoing projects include the Cossid moth which infects the Eucalyptus nitens trees used in commercial plantations. The moth bores tunnels in the trunk of the tree to lay its eggs. In order to control the spread of the Cossid moth, FABI engineered an artificial pheromone used to lure and trap the moths during their flight season. The sirex Woodwasp is another headache for the commercial forestry sector. This wasp attacks certain Pine species and FABI helped develop a biological control agent – a parasitic nematode that only feeds on the specific fungus that the woodwasp injects into the tree. This nematode is mass produced at FABI and then used to inoculate trees with. The Blue Gum Gall Wasp female lays her eggs in young Eucalyptus trees which stunts growth of the tree. So far 4 wasp parasitoids have been identified but they are still in the testing phase before these can be used in the field. But the FABI team are faced with a new challenge. Unlike many other pests who hone in on a specific plant species or family, the Polyphagous Shothole Borer (PSHB), is a sesame seed-sized beetle that infests more than 200 tree species from 58 families. The beetle bores into the tree and lays its eggs. But it is not this damage that kills the tree. The beetle travels with a range of symbiotic fungi and it is one strain of the fungus, which the larvae feeds on once they hatch that causes harm to the tree. The PSHB/fungus combination poses a threat to a range of tree crops, like avocado, macadamia, pecan, peach, orange and certain vines. It has also been found on indigenous species like cabbage tree, Outeniqua yellowwood, kruidjie-roer-my-nie, coral trees, monkey plum, some species of acacia, keurboom and paper bark. The biggest concern thus far is the threat to Johannesburg's urban forest. Many ornamental trees have been infected in the Sandton Parkhurst area, as well as in Soweto where 300,000 trees were planted in 2010 as part of the Greening Soweto project. The pregnant female beetle can fly up to 1km which facilitates the spread. Infestations have been found in Bloemfontein, George & Knysna. The PSHB was first discovered in South Africa in 2007 by Dr Trudy Paap at the KZN Botanical Gardens in Pietermaritzburg and she is still involved in the research. Meet the superheroes at FABI that are fighting this new threat: At the helm of fighting this PSHB are Professors Brett Hurley, Wilhelm de Beer and Noelani van den Berg . They also form part of the Ambrosia Beetle Working Group that has recently been established to bring various stakeholders together (Including DAFF, Joburg City Parks and the Plant Healthy Early Warnings System). Prof Wilhelm de Beer is a mycologist/fungal biologist that focusses on the fungal symbiont that comes with the borer beetle. This fungus is what actually ends up killing trees. De Beer oversees the DNA sequencing of the fungus to establish if different specimens found in different locations across SA (and the world) are indeed the same strain. Once the fungus is 100% identified they can work on finding a natural enemy. Prof Brett Hurley is a researcher focussing on insect pests in Forest Trees. He focusses on finding a biocontrol agent for the PSHB, by looking at factors such as host resistance (i.e. which trees the bugs DO NOT eat) and insect-microbe interactions. Prof Van Den Berg runs the Fruit Tree Biotechnology Programme at FABI. At the moment there are no infestations of fruit trees by PSHB in South Africa, and she and her team are working on keeping our trees safe – i.e. preventative measures. Together they continually monitor the spread of the beetle across the country, and assess the risks to crop trees, commercial forests and indigenous forests. Dr Paap is also based at FABI and is part of the International Plant Sentinel Network, which serves as an early warning system to notify scientists of new pests and pathogens to a specific country. The IPSN is an international network, linking botanical gardens and arboreta and plant health scientists. Dr Paap's work is all about detecting threats early so plans can be put in place to mitigate the threats. Scientists don't have all the answers yet, but the race is on to find out how exactly the symbiotic process between the PSHB and the associated fungus works and what makes some trees resistant and others not. Additional Info: Contrary to the Daily Maverick article, Joburg City Parks is quite involved behind the scenes. Adelaide Chokoe is the organisation's arboriculturist and is also part of the Ambrosia Beetle Working Group. The Joburg Tree Society is also actively involved, identifying affected trees, and feeding the information to FABI. At the moment the focus of the media is on Johannesburg City's trees. There are many worried gardeners and the idea is not to create a panic. Insecticides and fungicides DO NOT WORK, even though there are those on Facebook that claims it does. Affected trees need to be cut down, chipped or burnt to limit the spread of the PSHB. The greater concern is of course our tree crops and natural forests. In the USA and Israel they have experienced large die-offs of trees like Avocado as a result of infestation. There are some concerns about the widespread castor bean in the KZN region. It is an important reproductive host and could potentially act as a corridor for invasion across urban and agricultural habitats.
